title: Proof pages for a logistics company
metaTitle: Logistics proof pages that show the move
excerpt: Open a proof page with the constraint, the decision, and the move itself. A globe or a screenshot without a decision is decoration. End on how a similar operator requests a quote.
alt: A close view of a fountain pen writing on lined paper, the kind of specific record a logistics proof page should read like.
caption: A fountain pen writing on lined paper. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should a logistics case study open with?
faqs.answer: Open with the constraint that made the move hard, in places, equipment, and a clock. Name the decision a person made, including what it cost you. Put both at the top. Most readers will not reach a conclusion that waits under a gallery of trucks, and a map of the world does not substitute for the load.

faqs.question: Can we publish a case without naming the shipper?
faqs.answer: Yes. Mode, region, constraint, decision, and outcome are enough when a customer will not approve more. Say so plainly, and do not invent a quotation or a street to make it feel specific. A real nameless load is stronger than a fictional named one.

faqs.question: How should the page end?
faqs.answer: Tell a similar operator how to request a quote, which facts to include, and who the story is not for. Use the same quote label as the rest of the site. If the story depended on a favor you will not repeat, say that before they write.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
A logistics company case study page should show a constraint, a decision, and the work. The work is a move, not a globe. Screenshots of a dashboard with no decision are decoration. End on how a similar operator can request a quote.

Write it for the person who will tender the next load, not for a slide that needs a logo. They are asking whether you behave like this when the appointment is tight.

## Open with the constraint

The constraint is what made the move hard. A receiver who only takes freight before 10am. A machine that could not be stacked. A reweigh that threatened the rate after the truck was at the dock. A storm that closed the pass you usually run. If nothing was hard, you do not have a case. You have a testimonial costume.

Name places, equipment, and the clock in the first paragraph. "Eight pallets, appointment delivery, Chicago to a receiver who closes the dock at noon." Leave the customer's confidential price out if they did not agree to it. Do not leave out the difficulty. The difficulty is why a peer keeps reading.

Nielsen Norman Group's reading research is the cut. People have time for about a quarter of the text on a page they open. The constraint and the decision have to be in the opening and in the headings. A long scene of trucks at dawn, with the point in the last section, will be abandoned somewhere in the middle of the dawn.

One move per page. A collage of "we serve many industries" is the globe in prose. Choose the load that resembles the freight you want more of this quarter.

## Name the decision

A decision is a choice with a cost. You held the trailer overnight rather than miss the window and pretend it was transit. You called the shipper before you reclassed. You refused the load because it was residential and your page says you do not do residential. You sent a smaller truck when the site could not take a 53-foot trailer.

Write a subject. "The dispatcher held the trailer." "The estimator redid the rate before pickup." A sentence with no person is a sentence the about page cannot support. If you cannot say who decided, the story is not ready.

Say what it cost you. A held trailer is a truck that did not take another load. A phone call before a reclass is a slower yes. Operators are looking for that cost, because it predicts how you will treat their freight. A page that only records a happy POD reads as edited. It was.

Do not write a quote the shipper did not say. If they will put a sentence in their own words and approve the name, use it. If they will only approve a nameless paraphrase, paraphrase and skip the quotation marks. Invented praise is a worse risk than a plain account, especially in a business where people talk to each other at the same docks.

## Show the move

The move is the object. Origin, destination, what it was, what completed, what the operator received. A POD. A rate that held. An appointment that was met. A claim that was paid inside the window you publish.

Pictures come after the words, and only when they show the decision. A seal, a piece count on a bill, a temperature reading, a dock at the hour you claimed. A skyline, a container on open water, or a map with a glowing arc are the globe again. Crop to the evidence. If you cannot show the customer's freight, show your yard and your document with private fields covered, and say what was covered.

Label samples. A reconstructed timeline should say it is reconstructed. A real load should not borrow a neighborhood it did not visit. You do not need a last name. You need enough that a dispatcher believes the day happened.

One annotated image is enough. The line under it repeats the decision. "Held for the morning window. Receiver signed at 9:40." That line is the case. A gallery of twelve truck photos is a brochure.

## Numbers you can point at

Use a count you can find in a file. One load. A transit that matched the quote. A detention clock you honored. If you want a percentage, publish the denominator and the period. "Nine of the ten appointment loads that month made the window" is a different sentence from "99% on time," and the first one is the one you can defend.

Skip "faster than the industry" unless you can say which industry figure and how you measured. You almost certainly cannot, on a case page, without turning it into a different article. Write the clock you hit and stop.

Google's people-first guidance favors first-hand experience. Someone who worked the load should be the source of the sequence, even if a writer cleans the sentences. A case assembled from a marketing request and a stock photo will sound like a route that never left the building. The next operator can hear it.

If the customer will not allow detail, shrink the story. Mode, region, constraint, decision, outcome, with no street and no rate. Do not fill the gap with adjectives. Adjectives are how thin cases get long.

## End on a quote from a similar operator

The last block says who this story is for and who should not bother. Same label as the rest of the site: request a quote. List the facts that would let you price a similar move. Name the refusal that still applies.

"If you have palletized freight, a dock, and an appointment you need kept in this region, request a quote. Have the weight and the ready date. If you need a residential liftgate, this is not our work." That ending is useful to the wrong fit and the right one.

Do not end on the future of supply chains. The next step is a quote, or a clear no. Repeat the response clock you publish on the pricing page. If this story relied on a manual favor you will not repeat, say that too. A case that describes heroics you cannot staff is a trap for the next shipper.

Link the story to the service block it belongs to. A proof page for a mode you no longer sell should come down, or be labeled as history with no quote button. Archive is allowed. A quote button on a dead mode is not.

## Keep it shorter than a magazine

Four or five sections are enough. The constraint, the decision, the move, the limit of the claim, the way to ask for a similar price. Scene-setting about highways is how the page misses the quarter-of-the-text problem and becomes the globe with better grammar.

If you have three strong loads, publish three pages with three decisions. Do not merge them into one "success" page that asks the reader to assemble a company from fragments. Navigation can list the three by lane or by mode, in the operator's words.

Before design, remove the images and read the draft aloud. If the decision disappears, the images were hiding a hole. Put the decision back in a sentence. Then the images may return as evidence, smaller than you wanted, which is usually the right size.

## Walk the draft against the packet

Pull the load packet before anyone opens a design file: the quote, the bill of lading, the POD, and the exception notes. Highlight every fact the page states. Each highlight needs a home in that packet. A transit day that is not in the quote, a city that was only a relay, or a claim that you "always" call when the notes show you did not, should be corrected or cut. The page is not a place to remember the load as you wish it had gone.

Ask the dispatcher who worked the day to strike any sentence they would not say to the shipper. That sentence goes. Emphasis the desk will walk back on the next call turns a case study into a liability. The page should be something they can forward without a preface.

Then ask someone who books freight, and who does not know this load, what they are being asked to do at the end. If they say "be impressed," the close is still a trophy. If they can name the facts to send and the freight you will refuse, the page is ready to design. Keep their words for the labels when their words are plainer than the house style.

Check the clocks against the live pricing page and the service block. Free time, refusals, and the quote window have to match. A case that remembers last year's detention rule will be quoted back to you in a dispute. You will lose that argument in the reader's mind before anyone opens the tariff.

Read it once more with the photographs deleted. If the decision survives, the photographs can return as evidence, cropped to the fact. If the decision was living only in a picture of a truck, write it down. The truck can stay small.

A proof page fails if the operator cannot find it from the job they came to do. The labels for that map are [navigation for a logistics company](/blog/navigation-for-a-logistics-company).

If you want to walk a real load and see what the page should keep, book [an intro call](https://cal.com/hanabi/30min).
